title: Forces, density and pressure

parts.text:
11 The diagram shows a block of copper suspended in water.
face S
face R
The block experiences an upthrust from the water.
Which statement is the basis of an explanation for this upthrust?
A
Copper is more dense than water.
B
The area of face R is greater than the area of face S.
C
The density of water increases with depth.
D
The pressure of water increases with depth.

hints: Notice in the diagram that face R is deeper in the water than face S, so compare the water conditions at those two levels.
Recall how water pressure varies with depth through $p = h\rho g$ and how force on a face follows $F = pA$.
Compare the downward push on the top face S with the upward push on the lower face R to see which direction the resultant force must act.
walkthrough: Identify the useful detail: the block is fully submerged with top face S shallower than bottom face R in water of density $\rho$.
State the governing rule: hydrostatic pressure increases with depth as $p = h\rho g$, where $h$ is depth below the surface.
Apply it to the two faces: pressure $p_R$ at lower face R is greater than pressure $p_S$ at upper face S because $h_R > h_S$.
Convert pressure to force: water pushes down on S with $F_S = p_S A$ and pushes up on R with $F_R = p_R A$, with sideways forces cancelling.
Since $p_R > p_S$, the upward force is larger, giving a net upward resultant called upthrust, equal to the weight of displaced water. This is option D

A.explanation: Density of copper compared to water decides if it sinks, but upthrust exists for any submerged body and is due to the water pressure difference.

B.explanation: Face R is shown larger than face S, but the net upward force comes from greater pressure below, not simply from greater area.

C.explanation: Water is treated as incompressible here, so its density $\rho$ is effectively constant with depth and does not cause the upthrust.

D.explanation: Pressure $p = h\rho g$ is larger at the deeper face R than at face S, so the upward force on R exceeds the downward force on S.
